claims.text: The target alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr can be prepared as a near-perfect bulk crystal.
An oxygen content of approximately 1 wt.% matches the relevant experimental specimen.
The proposed approach separately computes temperature-dependent lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The lattice calculation uses ab initio anharmonic lattice dynamics and represents mass variation, force-constant variation, short-range order, and oxygen-induced distortions.
The electronic contribution is calculated from DFT-derived transport properties.
The approach is applicable from 200 to 1200 K for samples with minimal extrinsic defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are comparable near 200 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
The total thermal conductivity of an approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen is 10–17 W/(m K) in the high-temperature measurement regime extending to 1200 K.
Anharmonic interactions, oxygen-induced distortions, and short-range-order fluctuations affect phonon scattering and electronic states.
Separating lattice and electronic transport allows temperature-dependent force constants and electron-phonon coupling to be represented more accurately than in earlier approaches.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will remain within ±10% of experimentally determined values throughout 200–1200 K.
Combining the separately calculated lattice and electronic contributions will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% over previous techniques.
Earlier Debye-based, defect-free-crystal models typically have errors greater than 15% for HfNbTaTiZr over the same temperature range.
The hypothesis applies only to near-perfect bulk high-entropy alloys of similar composition and oxygen content.
High defect densities or different impurity levels may produce behavior not captured by the model.
Oxygen-induced scattering and low-temperature partitioning of lattice and electronic contributions remain uncertain.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or laser-flash analysis can provide an independently measured lattice thermal conductivity for the proposed comparison.
Electrical resistivity combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law can be used to estimate the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
The hypothesis is falsified by a lattice-conductivity error greater than ±10% at any tested temperature or by an accuracy improvement below 15–20% relative to the baseline methods.
